918.title: Envy at work
918.hook: a colleague's success, and the price they paid for it
918.howItsDone: Buddhists cultivate muditā, gladness at others' good fortune, as one of the four brahmaviharas, often in meditation; Christians read Romans 12:15 as a call to share in others' joy and grief.

segments.voice: Yesterday, ambition, examined: James and John asked for the best seats, and Jesus turned greatness into service. Your line was what is it for. What did one goal answer when you asked? Day nine hundred eighteen.

"A sound heart is the life of the flesh: but envy the rottenness of the bones." That's the book of Proverbs, in the King James Bible, and it could hang on an office wall. The announcement goes out. Someone else got the role, the bonus, the project everyone wanted. The congratulations in the chat arrive fast, a row of little hands clapping. Underneath, for some people, something slower starts to chew. It doesn't make a sound. It just sits in the bones, the way Proverbs says. Today: muditā.
screen: `ENVY THE ROTTENNESS OF THE BONES.` → `SOMEONE ELSE GOT IT.` → `ENVY AT WORK.`

segments.voice: First, an old voice that found envy inside work itself. Ecclesiastes says, "Again, I considered all travail, and every right work, that for this a man is envied of his neighbour." Notice the word right. Not bad work. Good work, done well, and the neighbor envies it. Envy isn't a sign that something went wrong at the office. It follows good work around. Second, the price. Envy looks at a colleague's win and skips the bill. The promotion may have come with late nights, a move, a missed dinner, a risk that could have gone the other way. Or it may not have. Often, we simply don't know. That's the trouble: envy works from half a picture. An honest question helps. Would I take the whole trade, price included? Sometimes the answer is yes, and that tells us what we want. Sometimes it's no, and the envy loosens. Third, a practice from Buddhism with a name: muditā. Buddhist teaching names it as one of four qualities to cultivate, along with loving-kindness, compassion and equanimity, and it means gladness at someone else's good fortune. It isn't treated as a feeling that arrives on its own. In the meditation manuals it's practiced on purpose, bringing to mind a person who is doing well and wishing that their good fortune last. Fourth, Paul, writing to the Christians in Rome: "Rejoice with them that do rejoice, and weep with them that weep." Rejoicing comes first in the line. Envy says their win is my loss. These voices say something else: their win is theirs, and a share of the gladness is free to anyone who wants it.
screen: `EVERY RIGHT WORK IS ENVIED.` · `ENVY SKIPS THE BILL.` · `MUDITĀ: GLAD FOR THEM.` · `REJOICE WITH THEM THAT REJOICE.` · then, large: `THEIR WIN.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and let the breath slow. Bring to mind a colleague, or a friend, whose success has stung a little. Don't push the sting away; just notice where it sits. Now think of what their win might have cost them, the parts nobody posts. You don't have to know; just allow that there was a price. Then, the way muditā is practiced, wish them well: may this good thing stay with them. If you pray, you can hold them in your own tradition's words. Before the bell ends, choose how you'll congratulate them today. The bell holds the time.
Muditā. Gladness at someone else's good fortune, a quality Buddhist teaching asks us to practice on purpose. Today's word.
Your line: their win. Congratulate one colleague today, out loud or in writing, and mean as much of it as you can. Day nine hundred eighteen.

919.title: A difficult boss
919.hook: a Stoic, a monk and a Sufi would each counsel something different
919.howItsDone: Benedictine monks and nuns live under the Rule of Benedict, which sets out how to receive and question a superior's orders; Stoic readers return to Epictetus's Handbook on meeting ill treatment mildly; Rumi's Masnavi is read and recited in Sufi circles.

segments.voice: Yesterday, envy at work, and muditā, gladness at someone else's good fortune. Your line was their win. Whose win did you name out loud? Day nine hundred nineteen.

An email arrives late on a Friday afternoon. The subject line is one word: urgent. Inside is an instruction that seems unfair, or unclear, or both, from the person who signs off on your work. Three old teachers would read that email very differently. A Stoic, who would try to read it from the sender's side. A monk, who would wait for the right moment to speak. And a Sufi poet, who would tell a story about a servant and a bitter fruit. None of them had email. Each of them knew about taking orders. Today: Luqman.
screen: `ONE WORD: URGENT.` → `A STOIC, A MONK, A SUFI.` → `A DIFFICULT BOSS.`

segments.voice: First, the Stoic. In his Handbook, Epictetus has advice for when someone treats you badly or speaks badly of you. Remember, he says, that they're doing what seems right to them. They can't follow what seems right to you, only what seems right to them. If they've judged wrongly, they're the one deceived, and the one harmed. Start from there, and you'll be mild toward them, saying each time: it seemed so to him. So the Stoic counsel isn't to win the argument in your head. It's to see the order from the side of the one who gave it. Second, the monk. The Rule of Benedict has a chapter for a brother given orders that seem impossible. He should first receive the command gently and obediently. If it truly looks beyond his strength, he should explain why to his superior, patiently, at a fitting time, without pride and without stubborn resistance. And if the superior still insists, the Rule says he should obey, trusting in God's help. Notice the order: calm first, then one honest word, at the right time. Third, the Sufi. In Rumi's Masnavi there's a story about Luqman, a wise servant. His master hands him a melon, and Luqman eats slice after slice as if it were sweet. When the master tastes it, it's so bitter it burns his mouth. Why didn't you say something? Luqman answers, more or less: I've eaten so much sweetness from your hand, how could I complain of one bitter thing? Rumi tells it as a lesson in gratitude toward God, and some readers hear it about people too. Fourth, the three don't agree, and that's useful. The Stoic sees the other side, the monk speaks up at the right moment, the Sufi remembers the sweet. None of them is advice to put up with cruelty or harm. They're for the ordinary hard instruction that lands on a Friday afternoon.
screen: `IT SEEMED SO TO HIM.` · `RECEIVE GENTLY, THEN EXPLAIN.` · `ONE BITTER MELON.` · `THREE COUNSELS, NOT ONE.` · then, large: `CALM UNDER ORDERS.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and let the breath settle. Bring to mind one instruction at work, or at home, that's hard to take. First, turn it around, the way Epictetus would: how might this look from the side of the person who gave it? You don't have to agree. Just say, silently: it seemed so to them. Then, like Benedict's monk, ask whether there's one honest sentence worth saying, and when would be a fitting time to say it. Last, like Luqman, remember one sweet thing that has come from the same place. If you pray, you can bring this to God in your own tradition's words. The bell holds the time.
Luqman. The wise servant in Rumi's Masnavi who ate the bitter melon without complaint, remembering all the sweetness that came before it. Today's word.
Your line: calm under orders. When the next tough instruction lands today, take one breath before you answer, and ask how it looks from the other side. Day nine hundred nineteen.

920.title: Mistakes at work
920.howItsDone: Readers of the Analects return to its sayings on faults as a guide to self-correction, and Jews and Christians read Proverbs 28:13 as a call to confess wrongs and turn from them.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a difficult boss: Epictetus sees the other side, Benedict's monk speaks at a fitting time, Luqman remembers the sweet. Your line was calm under orders. How did the hardest instruction look from the other side? Day nine hundred twenty.

The report has already gone out to the whole team, and the totals at the bottom are wrong. Nobody has noticed yet. There's a small window, about the length of a coffee, when the mistake belongs only to its maker. It could be fixed quietly. It could be left to see if anyone spots it. Or there's a hard message to send, just three words long: that was me. Old texts from two very different places have something to say about that window. Today: Zigong.
screen: `THE TOTALS ARE WRONG.` → `A SMALL WINDOW.` → `THAT WAS ME.`

segments.voice: First, Proverbs, in the King James Bible: "He that covereth his sins shall not prosper: but whoso confesseth and forsaketh them shall have mercy." There are two moves after the mistake. Confess it: say it out loud. Forsake it: stop doing it. The thing that doesn't prosper isn't the mistake. It's the covering. Second, Confucius. In the Analects he says, more or less: to have a fault and not change it, that is what's really called a fault. The first slip is ordinary. Hands slip. The real fault, for Confucius, comes after, in the refusal to change. Third, his student Zigong adds a picture. A noble person's faults, he says, are like eclipses of the sun and moon. When he errs, everyone sees it. When he changes, everyone looks up to him. An eclipse doesn't hide. It happens in full view, it passes, and the light comes back where everyone can see it. Fourth, putting it to work. Own it, fix it, learn: the phrase is modern, but the old texts hold each step. Proverbs says confess, which is owning it. It says forsake, which is fixing it and not repeating it. Confucius says change, which is learning. At work, all of this can fit into two plain sentences. I got that wrong. Here's what I'm doing about it. No speech, no long account of why it wasn't really your fault. Just the eclipse, in full view, and then the light.
screen: `CONFESS AND FORSAKE.` · `THE REAL FAULT IS NOT CHANGING.` · `FAULTS LIKE ECLIPSES.` · `OWN IT, FIX IT, LEARN.` · then, large: `I GOT THAT WRONG.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and let the breath slow. Bring to mind one recent mistake, at work or at home. Nothing dramatic is needed. Notice what rises: the urge to explain, to soften, to make it smaller. Let that pass by. Now, silently, try the plain sentence: I got that wrong. Then name one small fix, and one thing you'd do differently next time. If there's someone who should hear the sentence out loud, let their face come to mind. If you pray, you can bring the mistake to God in your own tradition's words. The bell holds the time.
Zigong. Confucius's student who said a noble person's faults are like eclipses: seen by all, then lit again when changed. Today's word.
Your line: own it. Today, if a mistake of yours turns up, say so plainly and early, before anyone has to find it, and then set it right. Day nine hundred twenty.

921.title: The craftsman's devotion
921.hook: in Japan, a craftsman's lifelong devotion to doing one thing well
921.howItsDone: In Japan, shokunin is the everyday word for a skilled craftsperson, and some speak of it as an ideal of patient, lifelong refinement; Catholic and Orthodox Christians, whose Bibles include Ecclesiasticus, and others who read it in the Apocrypha, find a similar honor given to craftspeople in chapter 38.

segments.voice: Yesterday, mistakes at work: confess and forsake, and Zigong's faults like eclipses. Your line was own it. Did the plain sentence, I got that wrong, get said out loud? Day nine hundred twenty-one.

A wooden box with no nails in it. The corners meet so cleanly that a fingernail can't find the seam. Somebody spent a long time learning to make a corner like that, and then made it again, and again, a little better each time. In Japanese, the ordinary word for a person who makes things with skilled hands is shokunin. Some people hear more in it than a job title. They hear a whole way of working, and a kind of devotion. Today: the craftsman's devotion.
screen: `A BOX WITH NO NAILS.` → `AGAIN, A LITTLE BETTER.` → `SHOKUNIN.`

segments.voice: First, the word. Shokunin is the everyday Japanese word for a craftsperson, an artisan: the woodworker, the knife-maker, the person who makes noodles by hand. When some people in Japan speak of craftspeople, the word can also carry a sense of character: someone devoted to one craft, who keeps refining it over a whole working life, and who takes the work personally, as a responsibility to whoever will use it. That second sense doesn't come from a scripture. It lives in how people talk. Second, an old book that honors the same kind of person. The Wisdom of Ben Sira, also called Sirach or Ecclesiasticus, describes the engraver cutting seals, the smith at his anvil, the potter at his wheel. The smith, it says, sets his mind on finishing his work and watches to polish it perfectly. The potter is always carefully set at his work. Third, Ben Sira's turn. These people, he admits, won't be sought for public counsel or sit in the judge's seat. Then he says that without them a city couldn't be lived in. They maintain the fabric of the world, and their desire is in the work of their craft. Fourth, what devotion looks like up close. It isn't perfection on the first try, and it isn't pride in being the best. It's returning to the same work and making the next cut a bit cleaner than the last. The attention points away from the maker, toward the work and the person who will use it. A bowl, a spreadsheet, a cup of tea, a lesson plan: each can be done the ordinary way, or a bit better.
screen: `THE EVERYDAY WORD FOR A MAKER.` · `SMITH, POTTER, ENGRAVER.` · `THEY MAINTAIN THE WORLD.` · `THE NEXT CUT, A BIT CLEANER.` · then, large: `A BIT BETTER.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and let the breath settle. Choose one ordinary task you'll do today: making coffee, folding a shirt, answering an email, sweeping a step. Picture yourself doing it slowly, once, with your whole attention. Watch your hands. Notice one small place where it could be done a bit better: a cleaner fold, a kinder sentence, a corner that meets. Not perfect. Just a bit better than the usual way. Let that one place be clear in your mind. If you pray, you can offer the task in your own tradition's words. The bell holds the time.
Shokunin. The everyday Japanese word for a craftsperson, and for some, a word for patient devotion to doing one thing well. Today's word.
Your line: a bit better. Do the one task you chose a bit better than usual today, even if nobody notices the corner that meets. Day nine hundred twenty-one.

922.title: Starting the workday
922.hook: a breath and an intention before work
922.howItsDone: Muslims begin ordinary acts with bismillah, in the name of God; some Jews and Christians pray Psalm 90:17 over their work; readers of Marcus Aurelius return to Meditations 5.1 on hard mornings.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the craftsman's devotion: shokunin, and Ben Sira's smith at his anvil. Your line was a bit better. Which corner met a little cleaner? Day nine hundred twenty-two.

A Roman emperor, writing notes to himself, admits he doesn't want to get out of bed. That's how the fifth book of Marcus Aurelius's Meditations begins: in the morning, when you rise unwillingly. Today the scene looks different and sounds familiar. The laptop opens, the inbox loads, and the first stretch of the day is gone before a single choice has been made. Several traditions put something small at that doorway. Today: Marcus Aurelius.
screen: `AN EMPEROR WHO WON'T GET UP.` → `THE INBOX LOADS.` → `SOMETHING AT THE DOORWAY.`

segments.voice: First, Marcus. His answer to himself is blunt: remember that you are rising to do the work of a human being. Why grumble about doing the very thing you exist for? Were you made to lie under the blankets and keep warm? Then he points outside: the little plants, the birds, the ants, the spiders, the bees, each working at its part of the world. Second, a psalm. Psalm 90 carries the heading a prayer of Moses, and its last verse, in the King James Bible, is a request about work: "and establish thou the work of our hands upon us; yea, the work of our hands establish thou it." The request comes twice in one verse, as if once weren't enough. If you pray, it's a line already made for the start of a workday. Third, a doorway from Islam. A hadith in the collection of Abu Dawud tells of words the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, taught for leaving the house: in the name of God, I put my trust in God, there is no might and no power except with God. Bismillah, in the name of God, is a phrase Muslim practice sets at the start of ordinary things, a meal, a journey, a task. Fourth, the breath. The Vietnamese teacher Thich Nhat Hanh taught people to stop and breathe before ordinary acts, even before picking up a ringing phone. Put these together and you get a very small practice. Not a ritual to adopt, just a doorway between the rest of life and the job: one breath, then one sentence. What is this work for, today? Then open the inbox.
screen: `RISING TO A HUMAN'S WORK.` · `ESTABLISH THE WORK OF OUR HANDS.` · `IN THE NAME OF GOD.` · `ONE BREATH, ONE SENTENCE.` · then, large: `BEGIN WITH A BREATH.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably, and picture the place where your work begins: a desk, a counter, a car, a kitchen, a classroom. Before anything opens, take one full breath, slower than usual, and let it out all the way. Then name, silently, the work ahead in a few words. Then one intention for it: careful, kind, patient, brave, whatever fits. If you pray, you can use a line your tradition already has, like the psalm's or the bismillah. Then let the picture go, and simply breathe. The bell holds the time.
Marcus Aurelius. The Roman emperor who told himself, rising unwillingly, that he was made for the work of a human being. Today's word.
Your line: begin with a breath. Before you open the first message or pick up the first tool, take one full breath and name what the work is for. Day nine hundred twenty-two.

923.title: Ending the workday
923.hook: a clear end protects the rest of life
923.howItsDone: Benedictine monks and nuns end the day with Compline and keep silence afterward; Jews and Christians read the close of the creation story in Genesis as a pattern of work that ends; readers of the Tao Te Ching return to its ninth chapter on stepping back when the work is done.

segments.voice: Yesterday, starting the workday: Marcus Aurelius rising unwillingly, the work of our hands, bismillah at the door. Your line was begin with a breath. Did the breath come before the inbox? Day nine hundred twenty-three.

The laptop is closed, but the work isn't. It comes along to dinner. It rides home in a pocket, buzzes during a bedtime story, and lies awake in the dark. A workday with no ending doesn't stay where it was put. It leaks into everything else: the meal, the friend, the sleep. The opening pages of the Bible tell a story of work that has its ending built in, and other traditions draw the line in their own ways. Today: Compline.
screen: `THE LAPTOP IS CLOSED.` → `THE WORK COMES HOME.` → `AN ENDING BUILT IN.`

segments.voice: First, Genesis. At the end of the sixth day, the King James Bible says, "God saw every thing that he had made, and, behold, it was very good." Then: "And on the seventh day God ended his work which he had made." Look at it, call it good, end it. In this story the ending isn't an interruption of the making. It's part of it. Second, the Tao Te Ching. Its ninth chapter warns against filling a vessel to the brim and carrying it full, and against sharpening a blade so keen it can't keep its edge. Then it says that when the work is done, withdrawing is the way of Heaven. Not hanging on. Not one more email. Withdrawing. Third, the monastery. The Rule of Benedict closes the monks' day with the night prayer called Compline, and after it, the Rule says, no one may speak. The day's work, and even the day's talk, gets a clear edge. Fourth, putting an ending into an ordinary job. It can be small. Look back at what got done, the way Genesis looks back, and let some of it be good. Write down what's left, so the mind can set it down. Then mark the line with a phrase, a closed door, a walk, a change of clothes. A clear end protects the rest of life: the people at home, the friends, the sleep. It also protects the work itself, which comes back the next morning to someone rested.
screen: `IT WAS VERY GOOD. GOD ENDED.` · `DON'T CARRY THE VESSEL FULL.` · `SILENCE AFTER COMPLINE.` · `LOOK BACK, WRITE IT DOWN, CLOSE.` · then, large: `DONE FOR TODAY.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and let the breath slow. Bring to mind the work of today, or of yesterday if today's hasn't begun. Name one thing that got done, however small, and look at it for a moment, the way Genesis looks back. Then name one thing left undone. Picture yourself writing it down for tomorrow, and setting it aside. Now say silently: done for today. Let the shoulders drop. If you pray, you can close the work in your own tradition's words. Then simply breathe. The bell holds the time.
Compline. The monks' night prayer in the Rule of Benedict, after which no one may speak, giving the day a clear edge. Today's word.
Your line: done for today. When your work ends today, write down what's left, close it on purpose, and say the line, out loud or silently. Day nine hundred twenty-three.

924.title: The commute
924.hook: travel time can be practice time
924.howItsDone: Jews say Tefilat HaDerech, the traveler's prayer, when setting out on a journey; some Buddhists practice walking meditation; Christians and Jews read Psalm 121 as a psalm for travelers.

segments.voice: Yesterday, ending the workday: it was very good, and God ended; silence after Compline. Your line was done for today. Did the work get a clear edge? Today, the last day of the week. Day nine hundred twenty-four.

A train car in the morning, rows of heads bent over glowing screens. A line of cars at a red light. A bus window streaked with rain. Between the start of the workday and its end there's a stretch that belongs to neither home nor work, and it's easy to treat it as time to be killed. Henry David Thoreau, in his essay Walking, says he has met hardly anyone who understood the art of walking, who had, as he puts it, a genius for sauntering. Then he tells a story about where that word came from. Today: the commute.

segments.voice: First, Thoreau's story. He says saunter comes from idlers in the Middle Ages who roamed the country asking for charity on the pretense of going to the Holy Land, à la Sainte Terre, until children cried, there goes a Sainte-Terrer, a saunterer, a Holy-Lander. Whether or not a dictionary agrees with him, his point is clear: a walk can be a small pilgrimage. Second, a psalm for the trip. In the King James Bible, Psalm 121 ends: "The LORD shall preserve thy going out and thy coming in from this time forth, and even for evermore." Going out and coming in: the whole commute fits in one line. Third, a prayer for the road. Jewish tradition has Tefilat HaDerech, the traveler's prayer, said when setting out on a journey, asking to be brought to the destination in peace and returned in peace. The road itself is treated as a place where something deserves to be said. Fourth, the steps. In the Satipatthana Sutta, the Buddha teaches that when walking, a practitioner knows, I am walking. Some Buddhists practice walking as a meditation of its own, attention resting in the feet. Put together, travel time can be practice time. Not every trip allows it in the same way: a driver's practice is full attention on the road. But a walk, a train, a bus, a passenger seat can be a stretch of quiet between the two halves of a day. This week ran through work's corners: envy, a difficult boss, mistakes, a craft, a beginning and an ending. The commute is the road that connects them.

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and let the breath settle. Picture the trip you make most often: the door, the street, the station or the car. Imagine making it once with the phone left in a pocket or a bag. What would you see? Let three things from the route come to mind: a tree, a corner, a face you pass. If you drive, picture the road itself, held in full attention. If you pray, you can bring the going out and the coming in to God in your own tradition's words. Then rest in the breath.
